name.text: Finding a point in the third quadrant

questiontext.text:
A point \(P\) on the unit circle lies in the third quadrant. The terminal side of the angle \(\theta\) passes through \(P\), and \(\sin\theta = -\dfrac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }\).

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The idea. \(P = (\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\) is on the unit circle, so \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) (Pythagoras' theorem with hypotenuse \(OP = 1\)). The identity gives the size of \(\cos\theta\), and the quadrant gives its sign. In the third quadrant \(P\) is to the left of the \(y\)-axis and below the \(x\)-axis, so both \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) are negative.

(a) Finding \(\cos\theta\)

Step 1: make \(\cos^2\theta\) the subject and substitute.

\[ \cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta = 1 - \left(-\frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{ {@sin_num^2@} }{ {@hyp^2@} } = \frac{ {@hyp^2@} - {@sin_num^2@} }{ {@hyp^2@} } = \frac{ {@cos_num^2@} }{ {@hyp^2@} }. \]

Step 2: take the square root.

\[ \cos\theta = \pm\sqrt{\frac{ {@cos_num^2@} }{ {@hyp^2@} }} = \pm\frac{ {@cos_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }. \]

Step 3: choose the sign. In the third quadrant \(P\) is to the left of the \(y\)-axis, so \(\cos\theta\) is negative:

\[ \cos\theta = -\frac{ {@cos_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }. \]

(b) Finding \(\tan\theta\)

\[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{-\dfrac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }}{-\dfrac{ {@cos_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }} = \frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} } \times \frac{ {@hyp@} }{ {@cos_num@} } = \frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@cos_num@} }. \]

Dividing a negative number by a negative number gives a positive result, so \(\tan\theta\) is positive in the third quadrant.

(c) The coordinates of \(P\)

The \(x\)-coordinate is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\):

\[ P = \left( -\frac{ {@cos_num@} }{ {@hyp@} },\; -\frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} } \right). \]

(d) The reference angle

The reference angle \(\alpha\) is the acute angle between the terminal side \(OP\) and the negative \(x\)-axis (green in the diagram). In the right-angled triangle, the side opposite \(\alpha\) has length \(\dfrac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }\) and the side next to it has length \(\dfrac{ {@cos_num@} }{ {@hyp@} }\), so

\[ \tan\alpha = \frac{ {@sin_num@}/{@hyp@} }{ {@cos_num@}/{@hyp@} } = \frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@cos_num@} }, \qquad \alpha = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{ {@sin_num@} }{ {@cos_num@} }\right) \approx {@ref_disp@}^\circ. \]

Since \(\theta\) is in the third quadrant, \(\theta = 180^\circ + \alpha \approx 180^\circ + {@ref_disp@}^\circ = {@theta_disp@}^\circ\).

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\). In the third quadrant, is \(P\) to the left or to the right of the \(y\)-axis?
Your answer has the same size as \(\sin\theta\). Use the identity \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) to find the size of \(\cos\theta\).
Your answer looks like the value of \(\cos^2\theta\). You still need to take the square root to find \(\cos\theta\).

falsefeedback.text: Use \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\): make \(\cos^2\theta\) the subject, substitute the value of \(\sin\theta\) and take the square root. Then use the quadrant to choose the sign.

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. In the third quadrant \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) are both negative. What sign do you get when you divide one by the other?
It looks as if you have divided the wrong way round. \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).

falsefeedback.text: Use \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) with the given value of \(\sin\theta\) and your value of \(\cos\theta\). Think about the sign of each before you divide.

truefeedback.text: It looks as if you have swapped the coordinates. The \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\) is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\).
Your \(y\)-coordinate is right, but your \(x\)-coordinate has the wrong sign. In the third quadrant, is \(P\) to the left or to the right of the \(y\)-axis?
Your \(x\)-coordinate is right, but your \(y\)-coordinate has the wrong sign. Check the value of \(\sin\theta\) given in the question.
Both of your signs are wrong: your point is in the first quadrant, not the third. In the third quadrant both coordinates are negative.

falsefeedback.text: Write \(P\) as \([\cos\theta, \sin\theta]\): use the given value of \(\sin\theta\) and your value of \(\cos\theta\) from part (a).

node.description: Gave theta instead of the reference angle

truefeedback.text: That looks like the angle \(\theta\) itself. The reference angle is the acute angle between \(OP\) and the \(x\)-axis, so it is less than \(90^\circ\).

node.description: Used cos/sin: the other acute angle

truefeedback.text: That is the other acute angle in the triangle. The reference angle is at \(O\), between \(OP\) and the \(x\)-axis: the side opposite it is the vertical side, \(|\sin\theta|\).
Your answer looks like an angle in radians. Set your calculator to degrees and try again.

falsefeedback.text: In the right-angled triangle, \(\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|\sin\theta|}{|\cos\theta|}\). Use your calculator (in degree mode) to find \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}(\dots)\), and round to \(1\) decimal place.
